https://www.politico.eu/article/donald-t.text: U.S. President Donald Trump and his top officials are slamming Spain over the migrant crisis unfolding in Ceuta, after about 50,000 migrants crossed into the northern African exclave from Morocco since Wednesday. “I saw Spain yesterday, and I watched the catastrophe that took place. It looks like an invasion of a country,” said Trump at a cabinet meeting on Friday. “Hundreds of thousands of people. And that same thing’s going to happen to us if the Republicans don’t get elected, except worse, much bigger, much easier to get into.” The U.S. Department of State was more categorical in laying the blame squarely on the Socialist administration of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez. Advertisement Advertisement “This unacceptable incident is the direct result of the Spanish Government’s deliberate efforts to enable and facilitate mass illegal migration into Europe. We are considering actions to defend Americans at home and abroad from this threat and stand ready to assist other European allies considering similar options,” wrote the department. Sánchez will hardly be surprised by the scathing American reaction, having emerged as the fiercest Trump critic among EU leaders, slamming U.S. military action in the Middle East and barring U.S. military planes from using Spanish air bases . “Thank God POTUS was elected and our country’s border no longer looks like this. These images out of Spain are an unfortunate reminder of the consequences of mass migration and the radical left-wing globalist policies that have enabled the Invasion of the West,” wrote U.S. Vice President JD Vance. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security made the same argument, saying: “If Spain had their own President Trump, this wouldn’t be an issue.” The U.S. criticism came as the situation in Ceuta escalated into a Europe-wide political flashpoint in little more than a day. Neighboring governments moved to tighten their response on Friday, with France restoring border checks and Italy calling for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen area, exposing divisions over the bloc’s migration policy. Former Trump adviser and world’s first trillionaire Elon Musk initially shared a video comparing footage from the Ceuta migrant crisis with scenes from the 2013 zombie film “World War Z.” “Wow, the situation in Spain looks crazy!” he posted. Clarifying the comparison was a joke, he then shared footage from 2023, showing hundreds of Venezuelan migrants attempting to cross into the U.S., captioning it: “This is what America looked like under Biden.” Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.politico.eu/article/russia-k.text: Russian authorities said Ukraine’s overnight bombardment of the western Krasnodar region killed two people and injured at least 12. Andrei Kravchenko, mayor of the Russian city Novorossiysk, said the attack killed one child and injured eight people. Drone debris damaged four businesses and 21 residential buildings, including apartment blocks, he said. Krasnodar Krai regional governor, Veniamin Kondratyev, said on his Telegram channel that more buildings were damaged elsewhere in the region, killing one man and injuring four people. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the attack on Wednesday but insisted that Kyiv’s forces had targeted the naval base in Novorossiysk, which he called “the last major stronghold of the Russian fleet in the Black Sea.” Advertisement Advertisement “Our Palianytsia jet-powered drones, Neptune missiles, and unmanned naval systems successfully struck the designated targets. Hits on air defense positions, piers, and seaport infrastructure have been confirmed,” wrote Zelenskyy on X . “The occupation fleet and all the infrastructure supporting it will not be safe as long as Russian aggression continues,” he warned Moscow. Russia’s defense ministry said the country’s air defenses had intercepted and destroyed 502 Ukrainian drones over several regions and the Black Sea overnight. Moscow has stepped up its missile attacks on Ukraine in recent months, killing dozens of Ukrainian civilians, while Kyiv has hit back at Russian targets, including oil refineries and warehouses belonging to Russian e-commerce giant Wildberries. Last week, an intercepted Ukrainian drone crashed onto a Russian beach , killing seven people and injuring 40.

https://www.bursa.ro/drought-unveils-hid.text: The exceptionally low levels of the Danube, caused by drought and heat waves affecting Europe this summer, have brought to the surface remains that have been hidden underwater for decades or even millennia. Wrecks of German ships from World War II, the foundations of a Roman bridge built under Emperor Constantine the Great, and Ice Age mammoth bones are among the discoveries brought back to light by the receding waters. The phenomenon offers archaeologists a rare research opportunity, but it also represents a new signal about the extent of the drought affecting one of Europe's main waterways. *The Danube reveals what it has hidden for decades The Danube, Europe's second-longest river, is going through a period of extremely low flows this summer. Data recently presented by AFP, based on information provided by the European Copernicus observatory, shows that in July average flows fell to record levels on important stretches of Europe's major rivers. In the case of the Danube, around two-thirds of the segments monitored recorded in July the lowest flows for this month since the European monitoring system began collecting such data in 1992. Similar situations have been reported on the Rhine, Rhone and Po. However, the retreat of the water also has an unusual effect. As the riverbed becomes visible in areas that are normally under water, objects and buildings that have been abandoned for a long time are coming to the surface. Some are linked to Europe's modern history, others belong to much more distant historical periods. *German Fleet Wrecks Resurface One of the most spectacular images comes from near the town of Prahovo, Serbia. There, the very low level of the Danube has made the wrecks of German ships that were sunk in the river during World War II visible again. The ships were part of a German fleet that arrived in the area during Nazi Germany's retreat from the Balkans. To prevent their use by opponents, the vessels were deliberately sunk in the Danube. For decades, the wrecks remained largely hidden underwater. Now, some of them have begun to be visible again, transforming certain parts of the river into a landscape that resembles an archaeological site rather than a European trade artery. Reuters and other international publications have reported on the reappearance of the wrecks in the context of the current drought. The phenomenon is not without risks. War wrecks can be accompanied by ammunition or other hazardous materials, making the simple withdrawal of water a safety issue. *A Roman bridge built during the time of Constantine the Great In Bulgaria, the Danube River offered archaeologists another surprise. The extremely low water level revealed parts of the foundations of a Roman bridge associated with Emperor Constantine the Great. The construction was part of Rome's imperial infrastructure and was one of the most important engineering works carried out in this part of Europe. For specialists, the moment is a rare one. Under normal conditions, the remains are underwater and difficult to research. However, the withdrawal of the river allows the examination of some constructive elements that can provide information about construction techniques, the dimensions of the infrastructure and how the Roman Empire organized its communications in the Danube area. The discovery also shows how old the relationship between the Danube and the economic and military infrastructure of Europe is. The river was not just a natural border. Throughout history, it has been a thoroughfare for transport, trade, migration and military operations. *Mammoth bones brought back to light In other parts of the Danube, the receding waters have also brought to the surface the remains of prehistoric animals. Among them are bones attributed to mammoths that lived in the region during the Ice Age. The discoveries are important for researchers because they provide clues about the fauna and natural environment of this part of Europe thousands of years ago. Thus, the same drought that reveals shipwrecks from the 20th century can reveal, a few kilometers away, traces of a world that disappeared long before the emergence of modern civilizations. The Danube thus becomes a layered archive of the continent's history. *From ancient Rome to the Second World War The succession of discoveries is unusual precisely because of their diversity. In a single period of extremely low water, traces of completely different eras can be observed: Roman remains, medieval constructions, commercial and military wrecks, but also prehistoric remains. In Croatia, for example, the retreat of the waters allowed obse rving the wreck of the Hungarian freighter Fulton, sunk in the Danube. At other points on the river, various structures and objects that are normally covered by water have become visible. For the public, the images are spectacular. For the authorities, however, the situation is more complicated. Historical objects can be damaged by exposure to air, and some of the wrecks can pose risks. In addition, the return of water can hide the remains again before specialists can complete their research. *A temporary window for archaeologists Low water levels offer researchers what can be considered a temporary archaeological window. Sites that are normally inaccessible become visible for a short time. Specialists can take measurements, document structures and analyze objects that would otherwise require expensive underwater operations. The problem is that this window can be very short. A change in the hydrological regime, a few days of precipitation or an increase in upstream flows can cover the remains again. In addition, exposure to air and rapid variations in humidity can accelerate the degradation of certain materials, especially wood, textiles or some metal components. For this reason, archaeologists must quickly take advantage of the periods when the river level allows access to these vestiges. Perhaps the most unusual consequence of the drought, however, is the transformation of the Danube into a true time capsule. As the water recedes, the river shows what it has hidden. War wrecks speak of Europe of the last century. Roman bridges speak of the period when the Roman Empire controlled the region. Mammoth bones refer to a prehistoric world, long before the emergence of states and cities. All these historical layers are now temporarily located in the same landscape. It is an unusual spectacle, but one that comes with a price. Articol despre History, Danube, water, archaeology.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Kash Patel, the FBI director. Photograph: Evan Vucci/Reuters View image in fullscreen Kash Patel, the FBI director. Photograph: Evan Vucci/Reuters FBI FBI investigates breach of jobs website as hackers claim ‘very sensitive data’ stolen FBIjobs.gov offline on Wednesday as ShinyHunters group claims to have accessed records of agents and applicants Associated Press Wed 23 Sep 2026 13.25 EDT Last modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 15.24 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its jobs website as a criminal hacking group claimed to have accessed “very sensitive data” on nearly all agents and job applicants. “The FBI is aware of claims regarding unauthorized activity affecting FBIjobs.gov and is currently investigating,” the bureau said in a statement. The website, the main portal for prospective employees to learn about the FBI and initiate the application process, remained offline Wednesday morning. A message that circulated online from a hacking group known as ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for the hack. The message, directed to FBI director Kash Patel as well as the assistant director in charge of the FBI’s cyber division, said the hacking group had “compromised very sensitive data on almost ALL FBI Agents and individuals who filed an application with the FBI for a job”. The claims could not immediately be verified, and an FBI spokesperson declined to comment further. An email to an address associated with the organization was not immediately returned. In its message, ShinyHunters said it would give the bureau one week to correct or remove what it says are false allegations in an FBI public service announcement from May that described the organization as a “cyber criminal group specializing in large-scale data breaches and extortion”. That announcement characterized ShinyHunters as “threat actors” who often “use their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims”, commonly harass or threaten victims and “may falsely claim to have sensitive or compromising information, including embarrassing photographs or videos of victims, which frequently do not exist”. ShinyHunters said in its message to the FBI that it was “offended” by those characterizations and demanded that the FBI remove those claims. The FBI has been a common hacking target. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to TechScape A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives after newsletter promotion In March, the agency disclosed that it was investigating “suspicious activities” on an internal system that contains sensitive information related to surveillance operations and investigations. Also that month, a pro-Iranian hacking group claimed to have hacked an account of Patel’s and posted online what appear to be years-old photographs of him, along with a work résumé and other personal documents dating back more than a decade. https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/bu.text: By Leigh Anne Miller Plus Icon Leigh Anne Miller Managing Editor View All September 16, 2026 11:00am The House of Terror Museum in Budapest. Photo Jens Kalaene/dpa-Zentralbild/ZB (Photo by Jens Kalaene/picture alliance via Getty Images The House of Terror Museum in Budapest has been closed temporarily by Hungary’s culture minister, Zoltán Tarr, who has also fired the museum’s director, Mária Schmidt. In a Facebook post , Tarr said that the museum would reopen later this year “pending a review of the exhibition’s content.” The museum closure is part of new Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s attempts to rectify his predecessor, Viktor Orbán’s, control of state media and arts and culture entities. Magyar won a landslide election this spring, unseating the far-right nationalist Orbán after 16 years in power. Related Articles Blind Man Sues the British Museum Over Lack of Bayeux Tapestry Audio Tours Bon Iver to Release 10th-Anniversary Edition of Album with Elaborate Artwork Elucidated The House of Terror Museum opened in 2002, during Orban’s first term, and presented exhibitions related to Hungary’s fascist and communist history. According to the Budapest Times , the museum was operated by the KKETTK Foundation (the Foundation for Research on Central and Eastern European History and Society), which has also been dissolved by Parliament. The foundation’s website notes that, since 2002, more than 8 million people have visited the museum, which, together with its various affiliated institutes, also hosted conferences, published books, and organized exhibitions. When the House of Terror Museum first opened, the New York Times reported that its many critics accused it of being a “political stunt,” pointing to its overly polished retelling of violent history and haunting music. Schmidt, the former director, had also been an adviser to Orban. At the time, she was unbothered by the museum’s overt political bent, telling the Times that “The political motivation of those who work here is to show that the system of terror was terrible—the Communist terror was terrible. Today in Hungary you cannot use the word ‘Communist.’ People act as though that part of history never happened.” The museum’s website includes a banner on the homepage noting that the museum is temporarily closed “due to technical reasons.” Recent exhibitions include paintings by József Ringhoffer depicting his experience of the uprising at Tiszalök, a forced-labor camp, in 1953, and an exhibition of photographs from the museum’s collection documenting the 1965 Hungarian Revolution.
